In June 2018, the Trump Administration released its own 132-page 
blueprint for government reorganization, entitled “Delivering Government 
Solutions in the 21st Century,” which would “touch virtually every agency 
and the way all Americans receive government services.” Charles S. Clark 
White House Proposes a Massive Reorganization of Federal Agencies, Go v ’T 
Ex e c u t iv e (June 21, 2018), https://www.govexec.com/management/2018/ 
06/trump-reorganization-plan-would-merge-education-and-labor-recast- 
hhs/149183/. Given the fate of the Obama Administration’s more narrowly 
targeted effort, the persistent institutional reality identified by Dean Kettl, 
and the policy trade-offs involved in any significant reorganization, the 
odds of legislative approval for so comprehensive a plan were never 
favorable. Because organizational consohdations also produce institutional 
ruptures, there may well be few government reorganizations that come to 
be regarded as unambiguously desirable. See MARIANO-FLORENTINO 
Cu e l l a r , Go v e r n in g Se c u r it y : Th e Hid d e n Or ig in s o f Ame r ic a n  
Se c u r it y Ag e n c ie s (2013). As of mid-2024, although the Biden 
Adminisf.ratinn created numerous working groups to deliberate policy 
across multiple agencies, it has advanced no significant proposal for 
government reorganization.
The Executive Office of the President (EOP), The Executive Office of 
the President sits atop the federal bureaucracy as a kind of mini-
bureaucracy comprising well over a thousand employees whose job is 
essentially to help the president manage the rest of the executive 
establishment. In keeping with the narrower scope of federal activity in the 
early Republic, presidents originally had no such help. As explained in the 
study cited above, which was commissioned by the Administrative 
Conference of the United States (ACUS): “Early presidents paid for White 
House staff from their personal salaries. Congress did not appropriate 
money for presidential staff until 1857. Historically, presidential staffs 
were small, comprised of secretaries, clerks, stenographers, and 
messengers. Presidents often employed relatives or acquaintances to work 
for them in the White House.” JENNIFER L. SELIN AND DAVID E. LEWIS, 
So u r c e b o o k  OF Un it e d  St a t e s  Ex e c u t iv e Ag e n c ie s 18-19 (2ded. 2018). 
Congress in 1939 finally authorized the creation a permanent professional 
staff formally attached to the presidency; since then, there has been a 
steady accretion of new functions as various areas of federal initiative, such 
as environmental or drug pohey, appeared to call for additional assistance 
at the White House level in coordinating a coherent government approach.
